prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: defendant officer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

**The Officer is entitled to qualified immunity because using a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.**

Qualified immunity protects officers unless (1) they violated a constitutional right that (2) was clearly established when they acted. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 232 (2009). This Court may begin with either prong. *Id.* at 236. A right is clearly established only if existing precedent places the question "beyond debate." *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011). Plaintiff bears the burden of showing that the right was clearly established. The right must also be defined with specificity, not "at a high level of generality." *Id.* at 742. Plaintiff cannot meet that burden here.

**A. Force is measured by the suspect's resistance.**

Excessive-force claims are judged by objective reasonableness. The court weighs the severity of the crime, the threat to officers or others, and whether the suspect "is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight." *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989); *see also Thomas v. City of Columbus*, 854 F.3d 361, 365 (6th Cir. 2017). The inquiry looks at the facts as they appeared to a reasonable officer at the moment of the force, not with hindsight. *Graham*, 490 U.S. at 396–97.

**B. This Court's precedent does not clearly prohibit tasing an actively resisting suspect.**

This Court has repeatedly drawn the line at resistance. It has held that an officer may use a taser on a suspect who refuses to comply and physically resists. *See Hagans v. Franklin Cnty. Sheriff's Office*, 695 F.3d 505, 509 (6th Cir. 2012). It has also held that tasing a suspect who is resisting arrest is reasonable and does not violate clearly established law. *See Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638, 641–42 (6th Cir. 2015). These decisions show that, at the time of the incident, no controlling authority held that a taser may not be used on a suspect who is actively resisting.

The cases that denied immunity are all distinguishable. They involved suspects who were not resisting at the time of the force. In *Goodwin ex rel. Nall v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314, 326–27 (6th Cir. 2015), this Court recognized that a suspect's active resistance changes the analysis. It contrasted that situation with one where the suspect has stopped resisting or is subdued. *Roell v. Hamilton County*, 870 F.3d 471, 480–81 (6th Cir. 2017), likewise turned on the suspect's being restrained and not resisting. *Austin v. Redford Township Police Department*, 690 F.3d 490, 498 (6th Cir. 2012), reflects the same distinction. The right to be free from gratuitous force after resistance ends does not clearly establish a right to be free from a taser while resistance continues.

**C. The Officer's conduct falls on the permissible side of that line.**

The record shows that Plaintiff [refused lawful commands, physically struggled, pulled away, and/or fought the officers — conform to the record]. The Officer warned Plaintiff and used the taser only while the resistance continued. [Record cites.] The Officer stopped when Plaintiff complied. Under *Hagans* and *Rudlaff*, that use of force was reasonable. At a minimum, no precedent put the Officer on notice that it was unlawful. The Supreme Court has warned against defining clearly established law too broadly in excessive-force cases, where the officer must make a split-second judgment about how much force is needed. *See Mullenix v. Luna*, 577 U.S. 7, 12 (2015) (per curiam). A general rule against excessive force does not give fair notice to an officer facing active resistance.

Plaintiff may point to cases about non-resisting, handcuffed, or already subdued suspects. Those cases do not "squarely govern" the facts here. *Id.* at 13. Without a case that has materially similar facts, or an obvious violation, the second prong is not met. The Officer is therefore entitled to qualified immunity, and this Court should affirm or reverse accordingly.
